title: Newton's second law: why a loaded bike speeds up slowly
examples: Why do heavy things accelerate slowly?

explain.say: Imagine riding your bike with an empty basket, then with a big sack of rice on the back. Same push. Which one speeds up faster? You already know: the light one. Newton's second law turns that feeling into one neat rule.

draw.text: Newton's second law: why a loaded bike speeds up slowly

explain.say: See the forward arrow? That is your pedal force. The small back arrow is friction. Take one from the other and you get the resultant force, which means the overall force left over. That is what makes you accelerate. Which arrow wins here?

The pedal force wins! Here is the rule: force equals mass times acceleration, F equals m a. Mass means how much stuff something has, in kilograms. So acceleration is force divided by mass. More mass, less acceleration. What if you push twice as hard?

Look at this graph for you plus your bike, 100 kilograms together. A push of 50 newtons gives half a metre per second squared. Now see the dot at 100 newtons: 1 metre per second squared. Double the force, double the acceleration. That is why the line is straight.

marks.label: 100 N: 1 m/s²
marks.ask: Why does a heavier object accelerate less?

explain.say: You have got it! And 200 newtons gives 2 metres per second squared. Wow fact: a rocket gets lighter as it burns fuel, so the same thrust gives more and more acceleration. Challenge: a 50 kilogram trolley gets a 100 newton push. How fast does it accelerate?

marks.label: 100 N: 1 m/s²
marks.ask: Why does a heavier object accelerate less?

faq.a: Resultant force equals mass times acceleration, F = ma. A bigger force gives more acceleration; a bigger mass gives less.
The resultant force is the single overall force left when all the forces on an object are added up, taking their directions into account.

faq.q: Why does a heavier object accelerate less?
faq.a: Acceleration is force divided by mass. With the same push, doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
asks: Why are heavy things hard to speed up?

faq.a: A newton is the unit of force. One newton gives a 1 kilogram mass an acceleration of 1 metre per second squared.

faq.q: Why does a rocket speed up more as it rises?
faq.a: It burns tonnes of fuel, so its mass keeps falling. The same thrust divided by a smaller mass gives a bigger acceleration.
asks: Why does a rocket get faster and faster?

facts: F = ma: resultant force (N) = mass (kg) × acceleration (m/s²).
One newton is about the weight of a small apple.

quiz.say: A 2 kg ball gets a resultant force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
quiz.show: A 2 kg ball gets a resultant force of 10 N. What is its acceleration?
quiz.why: a = F ÷ m = 10 ÷ 2 = 5 metres per second squared.

wrong.1: That multiplies; acceleration is force divided by mass.
wrong.2: That adds the numbers instead of dividing.

quiz.say: The force stays the same but the mass doubles. The acceleration…
quiz.show: The force stays the same but the mass doubles. The acceleration…
quiz.why: a = F ÷ m, so doubling m halves a.

wrong.0: More mass makes the acceleration smaller, not bigger.
wrong.2: Acceleration depends on mass as well as on force.
